learn.title: Start with supplied sources
learn.body: Grounding means tying claims to material you can inspect, such as a project brief, documentation or an error log. Tell the AI which sources to use and ask it to identify the support for important claims.

learn.title: Separate fact from inference
learn.body: A source fact is stated or directly shown in the material. An inference is a conclusion drawn from it. Inferences can be useful, but they need a label and a reason. Do not let a plausible conclusion masquerade as a quotation.

learn.title: Retrieval has limits
learn.body: Retrieval selects possibly relevant material; it does not guarantee complete or correct evidence. A search can miss the right passage or return something outdated. If the needed source is absent, say that the claim is unsupported instead of inventing support.

learn.title: Trace a habit rule
learn.body: The supplied brief says: A habit can be completed once per calendar day.
steps: Source fact: each habit has at most one completion for a calendar day.
Inference: saving should check for an existing completion on that date.
Reason: the check would enforce the stated rule during saving.
Unsupported addition: the brief says nothing about cloud sync, so do not claim it is required.

learn.title: Make support checkable
learn.body: A useful citation points to a source and location you can open, with a short exact quote when helpful. Then read the passage yourself. A polished link or confident citation is not proof that the source says what the answer claims.
Use labels such as Source, Inference and Unknown. They show what is evidenced, what is reasoned and what still needs information.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a source fact if the brief says: Show the seven most recent entries?
choices: The brief requests seven recent entries
The app must use a remote database
questions.explanation: The number and recency requirement are stated in the brief. The other claims add topics that the quoted requirement does not address.

questions.prompt: A conclusion drawn from source material, rather than stated directly, is an \_\_.
questions.explanation: An inference is reasoning based on evidence. Label it so readers can distinguish the conclusion from what the source explicitly says.

questions.prompt: Match each answer component to its best label.
pairs: The brief requires one completion per day
A duplicate check could enforce the rule
The exact sentence beside its document name
questions.explanation: Facts come from the source, inferences draw conclusions, unknowns lack evidence, and citations let someone inspect the supporting passage.

questions.prompt: Put these source-checking actions in order.
steps: Identify the claim that needs support
Compare the claim with the passage
Label the claim as supported, inferred or unsupported
questions.explanation: Start with a specific claim, inspect the actual evidence and compare carefully. Label the relationship only after reading the passage.

questions.prompt: Retrieval returns no passage about a required backup feature. What is the best response?
choices: State that support was not found and request the relevant source
Claim the feature exists without evidence
Treat an unrelated passage as proof
questions.explanation: Missing evidence should remain visible. Retrieval can miss material, so requesting the right source is safer than fabricating an answer or stretching unrelated text.

questions.prompt: What label fits a reasoned conclusion that is not stated directly in a source?
questions.explanation: Call it an inference and explain the reasoning. This keeps a plausible conclusion separate from a directly supported source fact.
